abstract_ko: <abstract lang="english">This study argues that traditional approaches to Korean language textbooks are insufficient for explaining changes brought about by the widespread adoption of AI in educational contexts. Conventional Korean textbook development has largely been based on fixed curricula and unit-centered structures, in which learners follow predetermined learning paths designed by teachers. To address these limitations, this study reconceptualizes AI-based Korean textbooks as an educational transformation rather than a mere technological application. It proposes three core analytical concepts— adaptivity, generativity, and dialogicity—to explain changes in textbook structure, knowledge construction, and teacher–learner roles. Based on this framework, the study compares conventional Korean textbooks with AI-based textbooks. The analysis shows that conventional textbooks retain fixed unit structures and pre-defined knowledge, whereas AI-based textbooks dynamically adjust content and learning paths based on learners’ language use and performance data. In this process, teachers function as pedagogical moderators rather than designers, and learners become co-constructors of textbook content. By interpreting AI principles through an educational lens, this study expands discussions on Korean textbook development beyond technical descriptions. It suggests that AI-based Korean textbooks should be understood as a new textbook paradigm that calls for a reexamination of textbook concepts and development principles. Future research is encouraged to apply this framework to concrete AI-based Korean textbook development cases.

abstract_ko: <abstract lang="english">This study critically reconstructs the concept of EdTech (EduTech) in Korean language education amid the recent shift from digital transformation to AI-enabled learning environments. Using a scoping review and literature-based qualitative concept analysis, it maps how EdTech has been defined and operationalized and identifies the limitations of tool-centric definitions that overlook educational value for language learning. Based on the literature, EdTech is reconceptualized as a languageacquisition ecosystem in which interaction is intentionally organized and data-driven feedback continuously informs instructional decisions and learner support. From this perspective, platforms and AI-mediated services function not merely as auxiliary tools but as constitutive mechanisms that shape communicative contexts and learning trajectories. The study proposes three interaction design principles— contextual presence, multi-agent agency (teacher–peer–AI participation), and data-driven feedback loops—and offers an operational diagnostic checklist to clarify conceptual boundaries and implementation conditions. The findings suggest a shift from technology adoption to ecological design to support more personalized, interaction-oriented language acquisition.

abstract_ko: <abstract lang="english">This study re-examines the pedagogical role of corpora in Korean translation education in the era of AI, focusing on classroom applications in Korean language majors in Taiwan. It traces the shift from corpus-based translation to AI-assisted translation and discusses how translation competence and instructional goals are being redefined in AI-driven contexts. The study argues that corpus literacy remains a core component of translation competence, particularly for evaluating AI-generated translations, diagnosing errors, and justifying translation choices. It then categorizes types of corpora used in translation education and highlights the pedagogical value of multilayered corpora that integrate AI outputs, learner translations, and revised versions. Drawing on three classroom cases—tourism corpora, Korean drama corpora, and learner translation corpora—the study demonstrates how corpus-based activities can complement AI tools and foster learners’ critical thinking and translation awareness.

abstract_ko: This study examines the structural crisis facing Korean language education in U.S. universities in the Age of AI and explores ways to redefine the unique identity of in-person classes. Analysis of the 2021 AATK survey data reveals that advanced Korean courses remain largely confined to the traditional paradigm of proficiency management and functional refinement. This structure directly overlaps with the linguistic performance capabilities of AI, thereby undermining the functional legitimacy of in-person classes. In response, this study proposes redefining language as a social practice rather than a mere set of functional skills. It introduces the ‘Delegate-Amplify Model,’ which delegates routine tasks such as summarization and proofreading to AI while amplifying interpersonal interaction and the social responsibility of speech within the physical classroom. Furthermore, it suggests instructional designs that transform AI outputs into materials for critical analysis and specifies subjective learning experiences through interdisciplinary integration and metalinguistic reflection. This study emphasizes that the Korean language classroom in the AI era must be redesigned as an irreplaceable educational space that fosters subjective linguistic agency beyond functional mastery.

abstract_ko: The purpose of this study is to investigate Korean language learners’ experiences and perceptions of using generative artificial intelligence (AI) in learning Korean. An online survey was conducted with 112 university-level learners studying in Korea and abroad. The questionnaire examined learners’ usage patterns, perceived usefulness, self-efficacy, reliability, ethical awareness, perceived suitability, and learning concerns related to generative AI. The results indicate that learners frequently use generative AI, particularly for vocabulary, grammar, and writing, and generally perceive it as a useful learning tool. However, learners also expressed cautious trust in AI-generated information and strong awareness of potential inaccuracies. These perceptions suggest that the educational effectiveness of generative AI may vary depending on learners’ usage strategies and critical judgment. Ethical concerns such as plagiarism, privacy, and overreliance were commonly reported. Qualitative responses further revealed both learning benefits and risks, often accompanied by critical and conditional use strategies. These findings highlight the need for level- and skill-sensitive instructional guidance, AI literacy education, and clear ethical guidelines to support the effective and responsible integration of generative AI in Korean language education.

Using written data from the 2015–2023 National Institute of Korean Language Learner Corpus, proficiency-level differences were examined, and an automated program was developed to calculate individual scores against corpus-based reference values. The results show that the D-value effectively discriminates across proficiency levels, while lexical sophistication also demonstrates meaningful variation; lexical density is mainly informative at lower levels. These findings confirm the usefulness of lexical richness for quantitative writing assessment and highlight the potential of automated evaluation, suggesting future research toward an integrated lexical richness index.

abstract_ko: In recent years, advancements in generative artificial intelligence (AI) technologies have had a significant impact on various writing tasks, such as assignments, reports, and essays. However, existing writing assistance systems often lack support for the Korean language and provide limited AI-assisted features, making it difficult to offer effective writing support for Korean language learners. This study proposes StoryCraft, an integrated document editing platform designed to support Korean-language writing by combining conventional document editing with AI-assisted writing functions. The platform incorporates large language models (LLMs) to provide a variety of Korean text editing and proofreading features, such as example sentence generation, rewriting, summarization, expansion, style modification, grammar correction, and conversion between honorific and non-honorific forms. StoryCraft also allows users to perform AI-assisted writing tasks directly within a single interface without relying on external applications or platforms. Through the integration of multiple LLM-based writing support functions, the proposed system aims to improve the efficiency of the writing process and provide practical assistance for Korean language learners. The study demonstrates the feasibility of integrating generative AI technologies into a unified document editing environment to enhance Korean-language writing support. To determine the optimal LLM model for each text editing function of StoryCraft, we conducted performance evaluations using Korean text datasets from AIHub. Based on these experiments, we selected models that offer superior performance and low latency to ensure a seamless user experience.

abstract_ko: This study aimed to develop an automated scoring model for language diversity that includes grammatical diversity. First, based on an analysis of the correlation between 17 lexical diversity measurement in-dices and expert group grading results, the root type–token ratio (RTTR) (r=0.87)—which had the highest correlation coefficient—was selected as the language-diversity feature. Lexical and grammatical diversity were measured using RTTR, and using these as features, a linear-regression automated speaking assessment (ASA) model and a random-forest ASA model were constructed and assessed. A total of 592 spoken data samples from Korean learners were split 7:3 for training and testing. The results indicated that the R2 of the linear-regression ASA model was 0.767, and the classification accuracy of the random-forest ASA model was 0.938. These findings confirm that grammatical diversity should be used as a major feature of ASA models by reflecting the agglutinative characteristics of Korean. Moreover, ASA model performance is better when the model is constructed to match the evaluation method. The significance of this study lies in providing foundational data that are useful for researching and developing interpretable Korean ASA models.

Written texts produced by learners whose first languages are Chinese, Japanese, and English were drawn from the National Institute of Korean Language Learner Corpus. The predictive performance of conventional pre-trained language models was systematically compared with that of LLMs, and an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) based on Integrated Gradients was applied to examine the linguistic basis underlying model predictions. The results indicate that, among the conventional models, multilingual BERT achieved an accuracy of 80.04%, whereas KLUE-RoBERTa yielded substantially lower performance at 31.75%. For the LLMs, zero-shot accuracy was moderate—49.61% for GPT-4.1-mini and 58.54% for HyperCLOVA X—but improved markedly following fine-tuning, reaching 86.99% and 87.32%, respectively. Attribution analysis reveals that the models draw not only on explicit nationality-related cues but also on cross-linguistic transfer phenomena, including patterns of postposition use, orthographic errors, Sino-Korean lexical choices, and modality expressions. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of LLM-based NLI for Korean learner writing and underscore its potential for fine-grained analysis of learner errors and the development of L1-sensitive pedagogical approaches.

abstract_ko: This study examines Korean language teachers’ generative AI literacy and competence development within a technology acceptance framework. Drawing on survey data from 156 teachers, the study analyzes usage patterns and the perceptual structure underlying AI integration. Although 75.6% reported monthly use, engagement remained largely introductory, centered on text-based material production. Exploratory factor analysis identified three latent dimensions: perceived instrumental utility, perceived educational effectiveness, and usage self-efficacy (cumulative variance: 74.4%). One-way ANOVA revealed that perceived instrumental utility and self-efficacy varied significantly by proficiency level, while perceived educational effectiveness remained stable across groups, functioning as a pre-formed normative belief independent of experience. Multiple regression analysis indicated that perceived instrumental utility most strongly predicted teachers’ intention to develop AI competence (β=.494, p<.001, R²=.303). These findings suggest that sustainable AI integration in Korean language education depends less on cultivating abstract educational value beliefs than on enabling teachers to experience immediate, practical utility—making hands-on, context-specific training the most effective entry point for competence development.

abstract_ko: The use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in Korean language education is growing, yet beginner learners remain understudied. This study developed and evaluated a writing correction template designed for beginnerlevel learners of Korean as a second language. The research was conducted in three stages. First, two prompt strategies—zero-shot chain-of-thought (CoT) and Few-shot—were compared in terms of accuracy, consistency, and learner-friendliness; the Few-shot method produced more stable and comprehensible feedback. Second, a prompt-based proficiency classification module was integrated using graded vocabulary and grammar lists from the National Institute of Korean Language. Third, 500 beginner texts were analyzed using the template and compared with human-annotated errors. The template achieved precision of 0.948±0.002, recall of 0.649±0.003, and F1-score of 0.771±0.003 across five repeated runs, demonstrating stable performance despite large language model (LLM) nondeterminism. False negatives frequently involved particle omission and written-style register errors, whereas false positives primarily resulted from fluency-oriented overcorrections. Cohen’s kappa (0.56) indicated moderate agreement with human annotation. These findings suggest that a carefully engineered template can partially approximate human judgment, support level-appropriate feedback, and offer a scalable foundation for AI-assisted writing correction for beginner learners of the Korean language.

abstract_ko: <abstract lang="english">This study aims to examine the principles and directions of AI-based Korean language textbook development in the era of increasing integration of artificial intelligence in education. As AI becomes increasingly embedded in educational contexts, its role in language textbook development warrants reconsideration beyond that of a supplementary tool. This study explores the principles and directions of AI-based Korean language textbook development from the perspective of collaborative intelligence, conceptualizing textbooks as systems in which humans and AI jointly contribute to design and operation. The study proposes three interrelated principles: (1) textbook structures should be designed to support human–AI collaboration, (2) learners' language production should function as an input for ongoing knowledge construction within the textbook; and (3) textbook operation should be grounded in teachers' judgment and intervention to ensure pedagogical alignment and responsible use of AI-generated outcomes. By articulating these principles, the study positions AI-based Korean language textbooks as dynamic, human-centered educational infrastructures rather than fixed materials or fully automated systems.

abstract_ko: <abstract lang="english">This study explores Korean language teachers' experiences of using artificial intelligence (AI) in classroom settings, focusing on its uses, possibilities, and limitations. In-depth interviews are conducted with nine Korean language teachers, and the data were analyzed using a phenomenological approach. The findings show that AI is mainly used for supportive tasks such as translation, example generation, and instructional material preparation rather than for overall classroom instruction. Positive experiences include enhanced learner autonomy, improved task performance, increased classroom participation, and reduced preparation burden for teachers. However, challenges such as learner dependence on AI, inaccurate information, assessment difficulties, and concerns about the diminishing role of teachers are also identified. The results suggest that teachers' use of AI is closely related to pedagogical judgment, instructional design and reconstruction, and digital integration and regulation. In addition, constraints on AI use are associated with institutional conditions, including insufficient training, limited educational infrastructure, and lack of collaborative knowledge-sharing opportunities. The study highlights a need to understand AI integration in Korean language education as a process of reconstructing teacher professionalism.

abstract_ko: <abstract lang="english">This study explores how using AI to learn Korean affects Chinese learners' motivation (Ideal Korean Self, IKS) and their readiness to engage in online conversations (Willingness to Communicate, WTC). In the study, we first analyze survey data from 262 students, and then conduct interviews with 12 of them. The results show that while simply using AI gives students a slight nudge to speak up, its true power lies in boosting their self-image. When AI helps students visualize their ideal selves, their desire to communicate grows much stronger. The interviews confirm that AI acts as a virtual mirror: it allows learners at different proficiency levels to safely project and refine their ideal selves, giving them the confidence to step out of this reflection and into reality to authentically interact with real people online.

abstract_ko: <abstract lang="english">This study aims to propose concrete instructional methods that enable intermediate-level Korean language learners to independently perform language tasks by utilizing image generation capabilities of generative AI, thereby exploring its educational potential. To this end, Seoul National University Korean Plus volumes 3 and 4 are selected as primary texts, and four tasks are designed for use with ChatGPT: “Creating Video Storyboards” and “Creating Comics” focusing on narrative construction and colloquial expressions; “Learning Korean Passive Constructions” to visualize abstract grammatical concepts; and “Introducing Recipes” integrating writing and speaking skills. This study is significant in that it presents a blueprint for new Korean language teaching methods aligned with the rapidly evolving AI era. However, as the research focuses on proposing instructional approaches and exploring possibilities, future studies should incorporate empirical validation through actual classroom implementation and analyses of learner perceptions.

abstract_ko: This study aims to define the new media environment created by generative AI as “synthetic orality” and explores its impact on human epistemic vigilance. Drawing on Walter Ong’s orality-literacy theorems, this study argues that modern digital literacy has entered a stage of “synthetic orality”, where the dynamism of orality is maximized within the framework of written text. To analyze how real-time interaction with generative AI affects learners’ critical thinking mechanisms, this study qualitatively examined interaction logs between learners and a sophistical AI. The findings reveal that learners tend to suspend the textual rigor when verifying information sources, driven by AI's fluent oral interface and pseudo-social presence. Moreover, some learners mirrored the AI’s sophistical rhythm during counter-arguments, indicating a trend in which their thought structures were assimilated the generative characteristics of the AI. Based on these findings, this study diagnoses that the tradition of “reflective distancing” established by literacy is at risk of deconstruction by synthetic orality. Consequently, it proposes cultivating vigilance literacy as a new direction for literacy education in the AI era. This study holds academic significance by suggesting an integrated literacy education that maintains analytical power within AI-driven interactions.

abstract_ko: <abstract lang="english">This study reconceptualizes the Grammar-Translation Method (GTM) in the context of AI translation tools, arguing that the core premise of GTM criticism—that translation is merely a means of language transfer—is fundamentally undermined in the era of AI translation. Methodologically, the study adopts a literature-based theoretical inquiry, critically reviewing prior research on GTM, machine translation in language education, and Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) and Human-Centered AI (HCAI) paradigms, and synthesizing these strands into a new conceptual framework for advanced Korean language education. Drawing on the HITL and HCAI paradigms, the study proposes the concept of translational agency as a new educational competency for advanced Korean language learners. Translational agency consists of three sub-competencies: critical detection, evidence-based revision, and contextual decision-making. These competencies are developed through post-editing (PE) activities in which learners critically evaluate and revise AI-generated translation drafts. The study further proposes an instructional model based on reconceptualized GTM, focusing on the pedagogical contexts of honorifics, culturemes, and text genre in advanced Korean education. The study contributes to the theoretical literature by offering an early systematic attempt to connect GTM with AI translation theory in Korean language education.

abstract_ko: This study proposes and validates a condition-based method for automatically generating personalized pronunciation assessment sentences for Korean language learners. The framework integrates corpus-based lexical and sentence-ending patterns from general- and academic-purpose spoken corpora, learners’ first language backgrounds and topic interests, and pronunciation conditions derived from L1-specific error patterns; candidate sentences were generated with a large language model and filtered through rule-based automatic validation, with human review used as a reference. Of 720 candidate sentences, 716 were successfully generated and 623 were retained after validation, yielding a final acceptance rate of 86.53%. The validated sentences generally reflected topic-appropriate vocabulary and endings and included multiple pronunciation-relevant phonological environments, suggesting that the framework can produce structurally valid, learner-tailored assessment sentences for adaptive pronunciation assessment and instruction in Korean language education.

abstract_ko: This study explores development strategies for AI digital Korean materials aimed at ensuring flexibility. Language instructional materials development must account for the diverse characteristics of learners and the varied environments of educational fields. While developers have continuously strived to ensure this flexibility, paper-based materials have been constrained by a lack of adaptable methods and limited ease in module implementation. To address these limitations, this study proposes a design strategies for AI digital Korean materials to enhance flexibility. If modules that support diverse adaptation methods are designed, AI technology is utilized to provide a technical foundation for flexible modification, and offer user-friendly interfaces to ease the implementation of flexibility, it will be possible to provide adaptable Korean materials that can be utilized by learners worldwide.

abstract_ko: <abstract lang="english">This study examines the feasibility of genre classification in Korean learner writing using Logistic Regression and Linear SVM, focusing on three genres: travel essays, argumentative essays, and expository essays. It aims to identify not only whether these genres can be distinguished computationally, but also which linguistic features contribute to genre classification. For this purpose, 1,000 learner texts were selected for each genre, and two types of features were extracted: expression patterns and topic words. Expression patterns were identified using PMI and TF-IDF, and topic words were extracted using cTF-IDF. Based on a pilot experiment, 600 features were selected for the main experiment. The results showed that the baseline model achieved the highest overall performance in both classifiers. Under feature-based conditions, however, Logistic Regression performed best with the combined feature set of expression patterns and topic words, whereas Linear SVM showed slightly better performance with topic words alone. These findings suggest that topic words function as highly discriminative semantic features, while expression patterns serve as formal features reflecting discourse structure and rhetorical organization. In addition, analysis of top-weighted features and representative cases showed that genre classification relied on linguistic features associated with prototypical genre characteristics, whereas genre confusion occurred when features strongly associated with one genre were repeatedly used in texts of another genre.
